title: Urban Air Pollution and Time Losses: Evidence from Cyclists in London — Revisited
text:
Klingen and van Ommeren (2020) showed that ozone pollution reduces cycling speed in London, using 42 million Santander Cycles trips during 2013–2017. A 10 ppb increase in ozone (roughly the difference between a clean and a moderately polluted day) reduced average speed by 0.3–0.4%, with effects detectable at concentrations as low as 20 ppb. The paper used four complementary identification strategies to rule out confounding from weather, traffic, and cyclist sorting.
This repository extends the analysis to 108 million trips through 2025, tripling the original sample. The code replicates the original estimation and tests whether the ozone–speed relationship persists across a period that includes COVID-19, the Ultra Low Emission Zone expansion, and substantial changes to London’s cycling infrastructure. It does.

title: Urban Air Pollution and Time Losses: Evidence from Cyclists in London — Revisited
text:
Results
The within-day specification exploits hourly ozone variation within a given day, controlling for day fixed effects, day-of-week-by-hour-by-daylight fixed effects, flexible weather controls, and other pollutants. The table below compares the original estimate to our replication and the extended sample.

Using 5 ppb ozone bin indicators, both the replication and extension samples show a roughly linear decline in speed with increasing ozone, with effects becoming visible around 15–20 ppb, consistent with the original finding that the threshold is well below regulatory standards.

Estimating the model separately for each year shows that the negative ozone effect is present throughout the sample period, with no sign of attenuation. The wide confidence interval in 2021 reflects reduced within-day ozone variation during COVID-19 lockdowns.

title: Urban Air Pollution and Time Losses: Evidence from Cyclists in London — Revisited
text:
Data
The analysis uses three data sources:

Cycling trips: Transport for London (TfL) Santander Cycles, available from the TfL cycling data portal
Air quality: London Air Quality Network, hourly data from 5 monitoring stations (BL0, KC1, RI2, SK6, TH4), via the Imperial College API
Weather: Open-Meteo Archive API, central London (51.52N, 0.11W)

title: Joris Klingen
text:
Joris Klingen


CPB Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis


EconomistData scientistMusicianDeveloper




I’m an empirical economist working on how people travel and how they use energy. At CPB, I study household energy use and the effects of green technologies such as solar panels and electric vehicles.
Much of my research uses large datasets, like bike-share trips, taxi rides and even chess games, to answer questions about transport, safety, energy consumption and the environment. See Research for papers and work in progress.
I hold a PhD from Spatial Economics at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, supervised by Jos van Ommeren and Erik Verhoef. I studied at Tinbergen Institute, VU Amsterdam and University of Amsterdam, and visited Dan Graham at Imperial College London’s Transport Strategy Centre in 2019.
I’m also a musician: I play keys in Flamingo Hitmix and drums in Bovenburen, and I like to develop software that is used in these music projects (see Music).

HitNoteDmx
Turns MIDI notes into a live DMX light show, so the lights can be played from Ableton sets with MIDI clips or like an instrument. This is what drives our light show for Flamingo Hitmix.

 GitHub

A standalone app that plays the same light show live without a DAW, from a Novation Launchpad and Launch Control.

 GitHub

title: Research
text:
AbstractDOIwith Jos van OmmerenEnvironmental and Resource Economics, 2023


Medical research suggests that particulate matter (PM) increases stress hormones, therefore increasing the feeling of stress, which has been hypothesized to induce individuals to take less risk. To examine this, we study whether PMs increases the probability of drawing in chess games using information from the Dutch club competition. We provide evidence of a reasonably strong effect: A 10μg increase in PM₁₀ (33.0% of mean concentration) leads to a 0.5% increase to draw. We examine a range of explanations for these findings. Our preferred interpretation is that air pollution causes individuals to take less risk.






AbstractDOIwith Devi Brands and Francis OstermeijerEuropean Economic Review, 2022


We provide novel evidence on the effect of smartphone use on road accidents. We exploit variation in phone usage fees in the Netherlands following a change in European Union roaming regulations implemented in 2017. The growth rate of mobile data roaming increased substantially after the change, which allows us to estimate a difference-in-differences model where non-Dutch drivers from the EU are treated, while Dutch drivers serve as control group. Our results suggest that around 10% of vehicles involved in accidents can be explained by the use of smartphones, and that these accidents mainly happen on urban roads.






AbstractDOIwith Laila Ait Bihi OualiCities, 2022


This paper tests whether and to what extent the implementation of bike infrastructure increases the propensity to cycle overall and by gender. We use large-scale Citibike data recording customer behaviours for New York City for years going from 2013 to 2019. We find that dedicated cycling infrastructure increases women’s participation in cycling by 4% to 6%. This corroborates the hypothesis that both genders are more likely to take a transport mode when it is safer, with a larger response for the subgroup of women.






AbstractDOIwith Jos van OmmerenRegional Science and Urban Economics, 2020


We provide novel evidence of the immediate impact of air pollution on time delays in urban outdoor activities. We focus on ambient ozone, which is known to reduce lung capacity. We estimate its effect on cycling speed in London using several estimation strategies, and find that ozone reduces speed for concentrations above 20 ppb, which is far below the minimum threshold suggested by other studies. A 10 ppb increase in ozone concentration leads to a 0.3–0.4% reduction in cycling speed. Despite that most cycling trips are short, it seems plausible that ozone induces time losses of similar magnitude of other outdoor activities, such as walking.






AbstractDOITransportation Research Part A, 2019


This paper studies demand for public rental bicycles following local and temporary metro interruptions in Paris. I construct a unique data set by linking metro interruptions announced by Twitter communication by the Parisian metro operator to usage data on the Vélib’ PBL. I find that, as a direct consequence of a metro interruption, the consumption of bicycles within 1000m of metro stations increases by 0.17 bicycles per hour per docking station on average, and with 1.36 bicycles per hour per docking station during the first 30 min; an increase of approximately 15% and 22% respectively. Due to their effects on demand, metro interruptions increase the probability of empty stocks at docking stations with 15%. The findings highlight that cycling is a local net substitute for metro service, and that public rental bicycles can alleviate time losses stemming from interruptions in public transport.

title: Research
text:
Work in progress



Protected bike lanes, rerouting and cycling safety: Evidence from Manhattan


with Daniel Graham, Cheng Keat Tang, Jos van Ommeren and Erik Verhoef


Do protected bike lanes make cycling safer, or do they mostly move cyclists onto the protected streets? We study how cyclists reroute and how crashes change when Manhattan streets get a protected lane.




Buying time or buying ease? E-bike choice in New York’s bike sharing


with Jos van Ommeren


Do people pay for an e-bike only for the time it saves, or also to avoid physical effort? We study how Citi Bike members in New York choose between a free classic bike and a paid e-bike, uphill and downhill on the same station pair.




Do Passengers Punish Drivers for Bad Luck? Traffic Delays and Taxi Tips


with Jos van Ommeren


Do customers punish workers for bad luck? We compare how New York taxi passengers tip when their driver is slower than other cabs on the same route at the same moment with how they tip when all cabs face the same traffic.




Congestion Pricing and Road Safety: Evidence from New York City


with Junjie Lin, Cheng Keat Tang and Jos van Ommeren


Did New York’s congestion charge make Manhattan’s streets safer? We compare crashes inside and outside the charging zone before and after January 2025, taking into account that the charge also cuts traffic in nearby areas.
